content.title: About
content.content: Chicken tenders or strips are pieces of chicken breast that are coated with bread crumbs and fried or baked until golden and crispy. They are a popular quick snack, fast‑food side, and kid‑friendly meal. The product typically contains chicken meat, breading, salt, spices, and sometimes additives for flavor and texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first breaded chicken pieces appeared in the United States in the mid‑20th century as a chicken alternative to fish sticks.
In Russia, chicken tenders became widely popular after being introduced in the menus of global fast‑food chains.
A double coating (flour, egg, then breadcrumbs) is often used to achieve an extra‑crunchy crust.
Flavor variations include classic, barbecue, spicy, cheese, and herb‑infused versions.
Breadings can be made from whole‑grain bread or gluten‑free ingredients for dietary needs.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Chicken breast provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low fat when baked
items.content: Baking instead of deep‑frying dramatically reduces added fat content.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken supplies niacin, vitamin B6 and B12, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It also provides phosphorus, selenium and zinc, important for bones and immune function.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: The tender texture after cooking makes it suitable for children and people with chewing difficulties.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Pre‑made breaded products often contain high levels of salt; people with hypertension should limit intake.

items.title: Trans fats and saturated fats
items.content: Deep‑frying in certain oils can introduce trans fats and increase saturated fat levels.

items.title: Preservatives and additives
items.content: Some manufacturers add flavor enhancers and preservatives that may be undesirable for sensitive consumers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chicken tenders can be enjoyed hot as a standalone snack, served with dipping sauces (ketchup, mayo, barbecue, yogurt), added to salads, wraps, or incorporated into dishes like pasta. For a healthier option, bake them at 200 °C (400 °F) for 15‑20 minutes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen tenders in an airtight bag at –18 °C (0 °F). Once thawed, cook immediately and do not store more than 2‑3 days in the refrigerator. Store cooked pieces in a sealed container to prevent drying out.

egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-made-with-co.title: Egg omelet or scrambled egg, made with cooking spray

content.title: About
content.content: An omelet or scrambled egg prepared with cooking spray is a quick, low‑calorie way to enjoy a protein‑rich breakfast. The spray replaces traditional cooking fats, allowing you to cook without adding extra calories or oil.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cooking sprays are typically a mixture of water, fine droplets of vegetable oil, and emulsifiers.
Cooking eggs with a spray retains most of their nutrients, including protein, B‑vitamins, and minerals.
Eggs are one of the most affordable and versatile sources of complete protein.
The spray prevents sticking, making pan cleanup easier.
In 1976, cooking sprays began to appear widely on the market.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: One large egg provides about 6 g of high‑quality protein essential for tissue repair and muscle maintenance.

items.title: Low calorie content
items.content: When cooked with spray, an omelet typically contains 90–120 kcal, depending on the number of eggs and added ingredients.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs supply riboflavin (B2), cobalamin (B12) and folate, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Choline
items.content: The yolk is a good source of choline, important for brain function and liver health.

items.title: Healthy fat for nutrient absorption
items.content: The small amount of fat in the yolk helps absorb fat‑soluble vitamins A, D, E and K.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg white proteins.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Egg yolks contain cholesterol; people with high cholesterol should monitor yolk intake.

items.title: Sodium in spray
items.content: Certain cooking sprays add sodium; choose low‑salt versions if you watch your sodium intake.

items.title: Additive sensitivity
items.content: Sprays may contain preservatives or flavorings; check the label if you are sensitive to these ingredients.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat a non‑stick skillet, spray with cooking spray, pour in beaten eggs and cook over medium heat, stirring until set. Add vegetables, herbs, low‑fat cheese or spices as desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Best enjoyed fresh. If needed, store the cooked omelet in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Reheat with a light spray to prevent sticking.

content.title: About
content.content: Pumpkin muffin is a soft baked good made from wheat flour, pumpkin puree, eggs, sugar and spices (cinnamon, ginger, nutmeg). Pumpkin gives it a distinctive aroma, moisture and a bright orange color. These muffins are often served as a dessert or snack and are convenient to take on the go.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pumpkin is rich in beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.
Pumpkin muffins became popular in the US in the early 2000s as part of autumn and Halloween traditions.
Pumpkin is one of the oldest cultivated plants, grown for more than 7,000 years.
Recipes often use spices typical for pumpkin pie, enhancing the flavor.
Pumpkin puree allows reduction of oil in the batter, making the bake lighter.

items.title: Rich in beta‑carotene
items.content: Beta‑carotene is a precursor of vitamin A, supporting vision and immune function.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Pumpkin and whole‑grain flour provide fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs and whole grains supply B1, B2, B6 vitamins involved in energy metabolism.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with traditional muffins, pumpkin reduces the amount of saturated fat.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Spices such as cinnamon and ginger have antioxidant effects that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: The classic recipe uses wheat flour, which can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Added sugar raises the calorie count; individuals with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Despite the pumpkin, the muffin remains an energy‑dense food.

items.title: Possible additives
items.content: Some commercial versions may contain preservatives or artificial flavors.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pumpkin muffins can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, sliced and topped with cottage cheese, yogurt or nut butter. They pair well with hot tea, coffee or milk.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store muffins in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage keep them in the refrigerator for up to 5 days or freeze in bags for up to 2 months. Warm before eating in the microwave or oven.

content.title: About
content.content: Pecans are the edible seeds of the pecan tree (Carya illinoinensis), native to North America. Unroasted pecans have a mild, slightly sweet flavor and a crunchy texture. They are used in cooking, baking, desserts, and as a snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pecans belong to the hickory family and are closely related to the chestnut.
Indigenous peoples domesticated pecans more than 2,000 years ago.
The United States is the world’s largest pecan producer, especially the state of Georgia.
Pecans are a key ingredient in the classic Southern dessert pecan pie.
Unroasted nuts retain more natural antioxidants than roasted ones.

items.title: Rich in monounsaturated fats
items.content: Pecans provide a high amount of heart‑healthy monounsaturated fats.

items.title: Source of vitamin E
items.content: Vitamin E acts as an antioxidant, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Contains zinc and magnesium
items.content: These minerals support immune function, metabolism, and bone health.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Abundant antioxidants
items.content: Pecans are rich in polyphenols that may help reduce inflammation.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: Pecans can trigger allergic reactions in some individuals, potentially severe.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Because pecans are calorie‑dense, portion control is important.

items.title: Choking hazard for children
items.content: Whole pecans can pose a choking risk for young children and should be chopped.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: People prone to kidney stones may need to limit pecan intake due to oxalates.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Unroasted pecans can be eaten as a snack, added to granola, yogurt, salads, baked goods, or made into nut butter. They are also used in sauces and desserts. Soaking them for a few hours softens the texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store pecans in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent fat oxidation. Discard nuts that smell rancid.
